title: Sharding, and everything it costs you

spec.title: Sharding, and everything it costs you
spec.description: The last resort among scaling techniques, because it is the one that breaks the guarantees you chose a relational database for. Exhaust caching, replicas and federation first.

nodes.label: What you gave up
nodes.sublabel:
• joins across shards
• transactions spanning shards
• global uniqueness / AUTO_INCREMENT
• cheap resharding
• one hot key can still melt a shard

flows.name: A query the shard key answers

steps.text: The application asks for one user's orders. Crucially, the query carries the shard key.

The router computes the shard and touches exactly one database. Latency and load are the same as an unsharded system a third the size — this is the case sharding is good at, and the case you should design your access patterns around.

flows.name: A query the shard key can't answer

steps.text: Now the application asks for all orders placed last Tuesday. Nothing about that query identifies a shard.

The router must ask every shard and merge the results — scatter-gather. Cost grows with shard count, and latency is set by the slowest shard, so the tail-latency problem gets worse with every shard you add.

This is why the shard key choice dominates the design. Pick the key your most frequent queries already carry. Analytics that cannot use it belong in a separate system fed asynchronously, not in scatter-gather queries against your serving database.
Joins across shards stop being a database feature and become application code. Transactions spanning shards need two-phase commit or sagas with compensating actions.
AUTO_INCREMENT no longer gives global uniqueness — which is precisely why distributed ID generation becomes a problem you have to solve.

And resharding means moving data while serving traffic. Consistent hashing limits the movement to roughly 1/N of keys instead of nearly all of them, which is why it appears here too. Do caching, read replicas and federation first — all of them are cheaper than this.
